definition: A 1966 classification of computers by how many instruction streams run at once and how many data streams each acts on, giving four classes: SISD, SIMD, MISD and MIMD. It is a coarse vocabulary; real machines mix the classes at different levels.
example: A multicore CPU is MIMD across its cores, while each core's AVX instructions are SIMD.

definition: The sequence of instructions one processor (or core) fetches and executes. Flynn's taxonomy counts how many independent instruction streams a machine runs at once.
example: Three cores running a browser, a compiler and a music player are three instruction streams.

definition: In Flynn's taxonomy, the flow of data elements an instruction stream operates on. One instruction applied to eight array elements at once acts on eight data streams.

Single instruction, single data: Flynn's class for a processor that applies one instruction to one data element at a time. It is the mental model of a simple scalar CPU, even though real cores overlap work internally.
Multiple instruction, single data: Flynn's class in which several different instruction streams operate on the same data stream. It is largely an abstract class with few clear real examples.
Multiple instruction, multiple data: Flynn's class for machines with several independent instruction streams, each working on its own data. Multicore CPUs and clusters of computers are MIMD.
example: An 8-core laptop running eight different programs at once is MIMD.

definition: Single program, multiple data: a programming style in which every participant runs the same program on its own part of the data, possibly taking different branches. MPI programs and CUDA kernels are usually written this way.

Single instruction, multiple threads: NVIDIA's name for its GPU execution model. You write scalar code for one thread; the hardware groups threads into 32-thread warps and issues each instruction to the warp's active threads.

Gustafson's measure of speedup when the problem grows with the machine: how long one processor would take for the larger job, divided by the parallel run time. With a fixed serial fraction it grows linearly with the processor count.
example: With 10% serial time on 64 processors, scaled speedup is 0.1 + 0.9 × 64 = 57.7×.

definition: Speedup divided by the number of processors: how much of the ideal one-processor-per-processor gain you actually get. 1 (100%) is perfect linear scaling; values fall as serial work and overheads grow.
example: A 6× speedup on 8 cores is 6 / 8 = 75% efficient.

definition: Speedup that equals the number of processors, so doubling the processors halves the run time. It means 100% parallel efficiency and is the ideal that real programs approach but rarely reach.

A speedup larger than the number of processors, so efficiency exceeds 100%. It usually means the per-processor work got cheaper, for example because each core's share of the data now fits in its cache.
example: 9.2× on 8 cores is superlinear.

definition: In Amdahl's law, the share of a program's one-processor run time that can be divided among processors, written p and between 0 and 1.
example: A program that spends 90 s of a 100 s run in a loop that splits perfectly has a parallel fraction of 0.9.

definition: The share of run time that cannot be parallelised: start-up, reading input, a final merge. Amdahl measures it on the one-processor run, Gustafson on the parallel run, so the same percentage means different things in the two laws.
example: A 5% serial fraction caps Amdahl speedup at 1 / 0.05 = 20×.

definition: Running a fixed-size problem on more processors to make it finish sooner. Amdahl's law describes its limit.
example: Rendering one frame on 8 cores instead of 1 is strong scaling.

definition: Growing the problem in step with the number of processors, keeping work per processor roughly constant, and checking that run time stays flat. Gustafson's scaled speedup is related to it.
example: Doubling both the simulation grid and the node count, and seeing the same run time, is good weak scaling.

definition: A diagnostic proposed by Alan Karp and Horace Flatt in 1990: the serial fraction that would make Amdahl's law reproduce a measured speedup. If it rises as processors are added, overheads beyond a fixed serial part are limiting scaling.
example: A 6× speedup on 8 cores gives a Karp–Flatt value of about 0.048.

definition: Uneven division of work among processors, so some finish early and wait while the slowest one sets the finish time. It lowers speedup even when all the work is parallel.
Time parallel workers spend coordinating instead of computing: waiting at locks and barriers or exchanging messages. It often grows with the number of workers.
A synchronisation point that every participating thread must reach before any may continue. CUDA's __syncthreads() is a barrier for one thread block.

Messages the cache-coherence protocol sends between cores to keep their caches consistent, such as invalidations and line transfers when several cores write the same cache line. It consumes bandwidth and time that grow with sharing.
Message Passing Interface: a standard library interface for programs that run as many processes, often on many machines, and exchange data by sending messages. It is the workhorse of HPC.
A United States national research laboratory where John Gustafson and colleagues ran the 1,024-processor experiments behind Gustafson's law in 1988.
A wide CPU register that holds several values side by side, one per SIMD lane, so one instruction can operate on all of them. Widths are 128 bits (SSE, NEON), 256 bits (AVX) or 512 bits (AVX-512).
example: A 256-bit AVX register holds eight 32-bit floats.

definition: One element slot of a vector register, and the slice of the arithmetic hardware that works on it. The number of lanes is the register width divided by the element width.
example: 256 bits / 32 bits = 8 float32 lanes.

definition: The 256-bit x86 SIMD registers introduced with AVX, named ymm0, ymm1 and so on. The lower 128 bits of each are the SSE xmm register; AVX-512 extends them to the 512-bit zmm registers.
Arm's 128-bit SIMD instruction set, officially called Advanced SIMD, available on most Arm application processors. Types such as float32x4_t hold four float lanes.

Arm's Scalable Vector Extension: each implementation picks a SIMD register length from 128 to 2,048 bits (current Arm specifications require a power of two; the original allowed any multiple of 128), and correctly written code runs unchanged on any of those lengths. SVE2 extends it with more integer and DSP operations.

Fused multiply-add: one instruction that computes a × b + c with a single rounding at the end. Peak FLOP figures count it as two operations, and the single rounding can change results compared with a separate multiply and add.
example: Two 8-lane FMA units give 2 × 8 × 2 = 32 FLOPs per cycle.

definition: Floating-point operation: one arithmetic operation, such as an add or multiply, on floating-point numbers. FLOP counts measure work; FLOP/s measure speed.
example: A dot product of two 1,000-element vectors is about 2,000 FLOPs.

definition: Billions (10^9) of floating-point operations per second, a common unit of arithmetic throughput.
example: A core doing 32 FLOPs per cycle at 3 GHz peaks at 96 GFLOP/s.

definition: Trillions (10^12) of floating-point operations per second, 1,000 GFLOP/s. GPU and accelerator peaks are usually quoted in it.

A register holding one bit per vector lane that says which lanes an instruction should update. AVX-512 has eight (k0 to k7) and Arm SVE uses predicate registers for the same job, for example to handle the last partial vector of a loop.
Functions a C or C++ compiler provides that map almost one-to-one onto particular machine instructions, such as _mm256_add_ps for AVX vaddps. They give hand control of SIMD without writing assembly.
The short scalar loop after a vectorised loop that handles the elements left over when the count is not a multiple of the lane count.
example: For 1,003 floats in 8-lane vectors, the tail loop handles the last 3.

definition: A memory load whose address is not a multiple of the access size. Modern x86 vector loads such as loadu accept any address, but crossing cache-line or page boundaries can cost extra.

A C99 keyword on a pointer promising that, while it is in use, the object it modifies is accessed only through that pointer. It lets the compiler vectorise without overlap checks; breaking the promise is undefined behaviour.
example: void add(float *restrict a, ...)

definition: A dependency in which one loop iteration needs a result from an earlier iteration, so the iterations cannot run independently in separate lanes.
example: a[i] = a[i - 1] * 0.5f + b[i] has a loop-carried dependency on a[i - 1].

definition: Combining many values into one, such as a sum or maximum. Vectorising a reduction usually keeps one partial result per lane and combines them at the end, which changes the order of floating-point additions.
Regrouping a chain of operations, for example turning ((a + b) + c) into (a + (b + c)). It is exact for integers but can change floating-point results, because every floating-point addition rounds.

Compiler options (such as GCC and Clang -ffast-math) that relax strict IEEE floating-point rules: allowing reassociation, ignoring NaN and infinity cases, and more. They can speed code up and also change or break numerical results.

A compiler transformation that replaces a branch with straight-line code: compute the candidate results, then choose per lane with a select or mask. It lets loops containing simple conditionals be vectorised.
example: b[i] > 0 ? b[i] : 0 becomes a compare and a per-lane select.

definition: A vector load that fetches each lane's element from its own address, given a vector of indices. It handles scattered data but is usually slower than one contiguous vector load.
In NumPy, an array's element data type, such as float32 or int8. It sets how many bytes each element takes and which compiled (and possibly SIMD) loop handles an operation.
Shipping several compiled versions of a hot function (for example baseline SSE2 and AVX2) and choosing one at run time after checking which features the CPU and operating system support.

The x86 instruction that reports a processor's identity and supported features, such as whether AVX2 exists. Feature bits alone do not show that the operating system has enabled the matching register state.
An x86 CPUID feature flag meaning the operating system has enabled the XSAVE mechanism for saving extended register state. Code must check it, then XGETBV, before using AVX.
The x86 instruction that reads the XCR0 register, showing which register states (such as the AVX upper halves) the operating system saves and restores. AVX is safe to use only if those bits are set.
The Unix signal a program receives when the CPU meets an instruction it does not implement or that is not allowed. Running AVX2 code on a CPU without AVX2 raises it.
GCC and Clang options that choose which CPU's instruction set the compiler may use. -march=native targets the build machine, so the binary may crash with SIGILL on older CPUs.
The order in which one thread's instructions appear in its program. Memory models describe which program-order pairs other threads may observe in a different order.
One way of merging several threads' operations into a single sequence that keeps each thread's own order. Sequential consistency allows any interleaving and nothing else.
A tiny multi-threaded program, with a question about which final values are possible, used to pin down what a memory model allows.
example: The store-buffering test asks whether both threads can read 0.

definition: The litmus test in which each of two threads stores to one variable, then loads the other. Sequential consistency forbids both loads returning 0; x86-TSO and Arm allow it because stores can wait in a store buffer.
First in, first out: items leave a queue in the order they entered. An x86 store buffer drains in FIFO order, so stores become visible in program order.

An instruction stream the processor tracks with its own registers and program counter. A core with simultaneous multithreading runs two or more hardware threads, each with its own store buffer in the x86-TSO model.

A memory model that lets loads and stores to different addresses become visible out of program order unless the program adds barriers, dependencies or ordered instructions. Arm and POWER are weakly ordered.
Arm's memory type for ordinary RAM, where the processor may cache, merge and reorder accesses. Device memory, used for hardware registers, has stricter rules.
Memory whose cache writes stay in the cache and reach main memory only when the line is evicted. Ordinary RAM is mapped this way; the dirty line's eventual writeback is real DRAM traffic.
Memory-mapped input/output: device registers that appear at memory addresses, so ordinary loads and stores control hardware. Such accesses have their own ordering rules outside the x86-TSO model.

An instruction that stops the processor (and compiler) from reordering memory operations across it in specified ways. x86 MFENCE and Arm DMB are examples; they cost performance, so they are used only where order matters.
An x86 full memory barrier: no later load or store is performed until every earlier one is globally visible, which in effect drains the store buffer. It forbids the store-buffering outcome.
An x86 store fence that orders earlier stores before later stores. Ordinary x86 stores are already ordered, so it matters mainly for non-temporal stores.
The x86 exchange instruction. With a memory operand it is implicitly locked, so it is atomic and a full barrier; compilers use it for sequentially consistent stores.
Arm's data memory barrier instruction. DMB ISH orders memory accesses before and after it for observers in the inner-shareable domain; the ST and LD variants order only stores or only loads.
In the Arm architecture, the group of processors (typically all the cores running one operating system) that a barrier such as DMB ISH must keep ordered with each other.
Arm's load-acquire instruction: no later memory access may be performed before it. It implements C/C++ acquire loads.
Arm's store-release instruction: every earlier memory access is performed before the store becomes visible. It implements C/C++ release stores.
An Arm load-acquire with the weaker RCpc ordering (from the FEAT_LRCPC extension). It is enough for C/C++ acquire and can be cheaper than LDAR because it may pass an earlier STLR.
Arm's Large System Extensions (Armv8.1): single atomic read-modify-write instructions such as LDADDAL, replacing loops of exclusive loads and stores.

An atomic update built from a load that marks an address, a computation, and a store that succeeds only if nobody else wrote the address meanwhile, retried until it succeeds. Arm's LDXR/STXR work this way.
An ordering on a load: no later memory access in the same thread may appear to happen before it. Paired with a release store it reads, it makes everything written before the release visible.
An ordering on a store: no earlier memory access in the same thread may appear to happen after it. An acquire load that reads the stored value then sees everything written before it.
The strongest C/C++ atomic ordering and the default: acquire and release effects plus a single total order of all seq_cst operations that every thread agrees on.

The weakest C/C++ atomic ordering: the operation itself is atomic and each variable has one modification order, but nothing else is ordered. Suitable for independent counters, not for publishing data.

The litmus test in which one thread writes data then sets a flag, and another reads the flag then the data. Seeing the flag but stale data is impossible on x86 and possible on Arm without barriers or acquire/release.

A memory-model property: once a write is visible to any other core, it is visible to all of them in a consistent order (other-multi-copy atomicity lets the writing core see it early). x86 and revised Armv8 have it.

Independent reads of independent writes: a litmus test with two writers and two readers that read the two variables in opposite orders. Multi-copy-atomic models forbid the readers seeing the writes in different orders.
Data-race-free implies sequentially consistent: the guarantee that a program with no data races, using only locks and seq_cst atomics, behaves as if sequentially consistent.
In the C/C++ memory model, the link created when an acquire operation reads the value written by a release operation. It makes the releasing thread's earlier writes visible to the acquiring thread.
An atomic operation that reads a value, changes it and writes it back as one indivisible step, such as fetch_add. Separate load and store can lose updates when two threads interleave.
The 2011 revisions of the C and C++ standards, the first to define a memory model for threads, with atomics and memory orderings.
A C/C++ qualifier telling the compiler every access must really happen, for hardware registers. It gives no atomicity or inter-thread ordering. Java's volatile is different and does order accesses.
A tool built into Clang and GCC that instruments a program to detect data races while it runs.
example: Compile with -fsanitize=thread.

definition: A classic lock for two threads using only loads and stores of two flags and a turn variable. It is correct under sequential consistency but needs a fence on x86 because of store-to-load reordering.

Apple's translator that runs x86-64 programs on Arm-based Macs. Apple silicon chips such as the M1 support x86-style (TSO) memory ordering for translated code, which helps Rosetta 2 run multithreaded x86 programs correctly and quickly.
A later load completing before an earlier store to a different address becomes visible. It is the one reordering x86-TSO permits, caused by the store buffer.
NVIDIA's platform and C++ extensions for running general-purpose programs on its GPUs: you write kernels that run as many threads, launched as a grid of thread blocks.

The repeated processing block of an NVIDIA GPU. Each SM holds a register file, shared memory, warp schedulers and execution units, and runs whole thread blocks; a GPU has tens to over a hundred of them.
NVIDIA's marketing name for one FP32 arithmetic lane in an SM. It is not comparable to a CPU core, which fetches and decodes its own instructions.

A function that performs one piece of data-parallel or numeric work, such as an array add or a matrix multiply. On a GPU it describes what one thread does and is launched over many threads; in performance work, 'kernel' means any such hot loop. Not the operating-system kernel.
example: saxpy<<<blocks, 256>>>(n, 2.0f, dx, dy) launches a GPU kernel.

definition: All the thread blocks created by one GPU kernel launch. Blocks in a grid may run in any order and, ordinarily, cannot synchronise with each other.
A group of up to 1,024 CUDA threads that runs on a single SM, can share that SM's shared memory and can synchronise with __syncthreads(). Its threads are split into warps of 32.
example: A block of 256 threads is 8 warps.

definition: One logical thread of a GPU kernel, with its own registers and indices. Thousands run at once; the hardware issues their instructions a warp of 32 at a time.
A group of 32 consecutive threads of a thread block to which an NVIDIA GPU issues instructions together. Threads in a warp that take different branches cause divergence.
example: Threads 0–31 of a block form warp 0, threads 32–63 warp 1.

definition: A CUDA built-in giving a thread's index within its block (with x, y and z parts).
A CUDA built-in giving the index of the current block within the grid.
A CUDA built-in giving the number of threads per block in each dimension.
The position of a CUDA thread across the whole grid, usually blockIdx.x × blockDim.x + threadIdx.x, used to pick which array element the thread handles.
example: Thread 10 of block 3 with 256-thread blocks has global index 778.

definition: Single-precision a times x plus y: y[i] = a × x[i] + y[i] over arrays. A standard small benchmark and teaching kernel; DAXPY is the double-precision version.
Double-precision a times x plus y: y[i] = a × x[i] + y[i] on 8-byte doubles. With 2 FLOPs per 24 bytes it is strongly memory-bound.
The CUDA barrier for one thread block: every thread of the block must reach it before any continues, and shared-memory writes before it are visible after it.
A CUDA barrier for the threads of one warp named in a mask. Since Volta, warp-level communication must use it (or similar primitives) rather than assume lockstep.
Fast on-chip memory in each SM that the programmer manages explicitly and that all threads of one thread block can read and write. It is split into 32 banks; tens to a couple of hundred KiB per SM.
On supported NVIDIA GPUs (Hopper onwards), the ability of thread blocks in a cluster to access each other's shared memory.
A CUDA grouping of thread blocks guaranteed to run at the same time on neighbouring SMs, so they can synchronise and share memory. Available on newer GPUs.
The GPU's large main memory (DRAM such as GDDR or HBM), visible to every thread of every block. Much slower than registers or shared memory.
When threads of one warp take different paths at a branch. The warp runs each path in turn with the other lanes masked off, so the paths' times add.
example: An if taking 100 cycles and an else taking 60 cost a divergent warp about 160.

definition: NVIDIA's model since Volta (2017) in which each thread of a warp has its own program counter, so threads may run apart. Code must not assume the warp moves in lockstep.
NVIDIA's 2017 GPU architecture (for example the V100), which introduced independent thread scheduling and tensor cores.
Several threads executing the same instruction at the same moment. CUDA does not guarantee it for a warp, so it cannot be used for synchronisation.
Keeping execution units busy during a slow operation by switching to other ready work. GPUs hide memory latency by keeping many warps resident and issuing from whichever is ready.
A warp whose state (registers, program counters) is held on an SM, so the scheduler can issue its instructions without any context switch.
Resident warps on an SM divided by the most it can hold. Registers, shared memory and block limits each cap it; higher occupancy helps hide latency but is not a goal in itself.
example: A 64-warp SM holding 16 warps is at 25% occupancy.

definition: Combining the memory accesses of a warp's 32 threads into as few 32-byte sectors as possible. Consecutive threads reading consecutive 4-byte words need 4 sectors; scattered reads may need 32.
The 32-byte unit in which NVIDIA GPU caches and memory transfer data. A warp's request costs one sector for every distinct 32-byte block it touches.

One of the 32 independent slices of GPU shared memory; successive 4-byte words go to successive banks. When threads of a warp hit different addresses in the same bank (a bank conflict), the accesses are serialised.
example: Reading a column of float tile[32][32] puts all 32 threads in one bank: a 32-way conflict.

definition: Specialised GPU units that perform small matrix multiply-accumulate operations, in reduced precision, much faster than ordinary FP32 lanes.
PCI Express: the standard expansion bus linking a CPU to GPUs and other devices. Its bandwidth (tens of GB/s each way) is far below GPU memory bandwidth, so copies can dominate.
example: 4 GB at 25 GB/s takes 0.16 s.

definition: A CUDA feature that records a sequence of kernel launches and copies once and replays it, cutting per-launch overhead.
Combining two passes (loops or kernels) into one so intermediate results stay in registers instead of being written to and re-read from memory. It cuts traffic and launch overhead.
example: Fusing y = a × x then z = y + b removes 8 bytes of traffic per element.

definition: The main memory of the host computer, attached to its CPU, as opposed to a device's own memory such as a GPU's. Data must be copied (or mapped) across PCIe before a GPU kernel can use it efficiently.
CUDA memory accessible from both CPU and GPU through one pointer, with pages migrated or accessed across the link as needed.
NVIDIA data-centre GPUs: A100 (Ampere, 2020, 108 SMs) and H100 (Hopper, 2022). Their exact counts and rates vary by configuration.
32-bit IEEE 754 floating point (binary32): 1 sign, 8 exponent and 23 fraction bits, about 7 decimal digits of precision.
64-bit IEEE 754 floating point (binary64): 1 sign, 11 exponent and 52 fraction bits, about 16 decimal digits. C's double.
An 8-bit integer type, range −128 to 127 when signed. Used for quantised neural-network inference, as in TPU v1.
Multiply-accumulate: multiply two numbers and add the product to a running total (acc ← acc + a × b). The basic step of dot products and matrix multiplies; peak figures count it as two operations.
The TPU's main compute block: a large grid of MAC cells arranged as a systolic array that multiplies matrices.

A grid of simple processing elements that each multiply, add and pass values to their neighbours every clock cycle, so each operand fetched is reused many times as it flows through. The name compares the rhythmic data flow to a heartbeat.
One cell of a systolic array or similar accelerator: a small unit that multiplies, accumulates and forwards data to its neighbours.
A systolic-array schedule in which each PE keeps one output element and accumulates it while inputs flow past.
A systolic-array schedule in which neural-network weights are preloaded into the PEs and stay put, while activations flow across and partial sums flow down. TPU v1 used it.
Running an already-trained neural network to make predictions, as opposed to training it. It can use lower precision such as int8.
Adjusting a neural network's weights from data. It needs wider numerical formats than inference, such as bfloat16 or float32.
A learned number a neural network multiplies its inputs by. A layer's weights are read for every example, so reusing them across a batch reduces memory traffic.
A neural-network layer in which every output is a weighted sum of every input: a matrix-vector (or, for a batch, matrix-matrix) multiply.
The number of inputs processed together in one pass. In neural-network inference, larger batches reuse each weight more times per byte fetched but make individual requests wait for the batch to fill.
Accelerated Linear Algebra: Google's compiler that turns machine-learning computations (from JAX, TensorFlow or PyTorch) into code for TPUs, GPUs and CPUs.
Representing values with fewer bits, such as int8 instead of float32, to cut memory and arithmetic cost at some loss of accuracy.
Using different floating-point formats in one computation, for example bfloat16 multiplies with float32 accumulation.
Tera-operations per second: 10^12 operations per second (GOPS is 10^9). Used for integer accelerators, usually counting each MAC operation as two operations.
A hard (fixed-function) multiply-accumulate unit built into an FPGA, much faster and smaller than building a multiplier from LUTs.
Small blocks of on-chip memory spread across an FPGA, typically tens of kilobits each.
Tools that turn a restricted C, C++ or similar program into a hardware design for an FPGA or ASIC.
Getting a hardware design to meet its target clock frequency: every signal path must settle within one clock period.
In a hardware pipeline, the number of clock cycles between accepting successive inputs. An interval of 1 means one new input every cycle.
A processor built from an FPGA's configurable logic rather than fixed silicon, for example AMD's MicroBlaze.
The third generation of double-data-rate DRAM, common around 2007–2015. TPU v1 read its weights from 8 GiB of DDR3 at about 34 GB/s.
High Bandwidth Memory: stacked DRAM placed beside a processor in one package, giving very wide, fast connections. Used on modern GPUs and later TPUs.
An NVIDIA data-centre GPU from 2014 used as the GPU comparison in the 2017 TPU paper.
Intel's 2013 CPU microarchitecture, Intel's first to support AVX2 and FMA; the CPU comparison in the 2017 TPU paper.
The start and end of a pipelined or systolic computation when only some units have work, which lowers average utilisation for short jobs.
The fraction of available hardware capacity doing useful work over a period.
Sending part of a computation from the host CPU to an accelerator. It pays only if the time saved exceeds data transfer and setup costs.
Keeping data in an accelerator's memory across many operations so it is not copied back and forth each time.

A performance model by Williams, Waterman and Patterson (2009): a kernel's attainable FLOP rate is the lower of the machine's peak compute and its memory bandwidth times the kernel's arithmetic intensity. On log–log axes it looks like a roof.
example: At 0.5 FLOP/byte and 200 GB/s, a kernel can reach at most 100 GFLOP/s.

definition: FLOPs a kernel performs per byte it moves to or from memory (usually DRAM). Low intensity means the kernel is limited by bandwidth; high intensity means it can approach peak compute.
example: Vector add on doubles: 1 FLOP per 32 bytes, about 0.03 FLOP/byte.

definition: On a roofline plot, the arithmetic intensity where the bandwidth slope meets the flat compute roof: peak FLOP rate divided by memory bandwidth. Kernels left of it are memory-bound.
example: 1,000 GFLOP/s / 100 GB/s = 10 FLOP/byte.

definition: One of the limiting lines on a roofline plot: the flat compute roof, the sloped bandwidth roof, or lower ceilings such as peak without SIMD or bandwidth from one core.
The highest arithmetic rate a processor could reach if every unit did useful work every cycle: cores × clock rate × FLOPs per core per cycle. Real code usually reaches a fraction of it.
John McCalpin's standard benchmark of sustainable memory bandwidth, using simple vector kernels such as copy and triad. It counts useful array bytes, not write-allocate traffic.
Intel's performance analysis tool, which can measure FLOPs and memory traffic and draw roofline charts.
NVIDIA's profiler for GPU kernels, reporting detailed counters and roofline charts.
Performance monitoring unit: the hardware in a processor that counts events such as cycles, instructions retired, cache misses and branch misses. Tools such as perf read it.
The Linux perf commands that sample where a program spends its events (perf record) and summarise the samples by function (perf report).
example: perf record -g ./app; perf report

definition: A profiler that interrupts the program periodically, or every N events, and records where it is. The counts show roughly where time or events go, with low overhead.
The gap between the instruction that caused a sampled event and the instruction the profiler records, so samples can land a few instructions late.
Brendan Gregg's visualisation of sampled call stacks: each box is a function, its width is the share of samples that include it, and callers sit below callees. Left-to-right order is not time.
One opportunity per cycle for the core's front end to deliver one micro-operation; a 4-wide core has 4 slots per cycle. Top-down analysis classifies each slot.
Top-down category for slots lost because the front end (fetch and decode) did not deliver micro-operations in time.
Top-down category for slots lost because execution resources or memory were not ready. It splits into memory bound and core bound.
Top-down category for slots spent on work that was thrown away, mostly after branch mispredictions.
Top-down category for slots used by micro-operations that completed and were kept.
The extra cost of the first runs of a benchmark: page faults, cold caches, lazy loading and JIT compilation. Exclude it only when steady state is what you want to measure.
A processor lowering its clock to stay within temperature or power limits, which can make later benchmark runs slower than early ones.
A compiler optimisation that removes computations whose results are never used. It can delete a benchmark's work and report impossibly fast times.
example: 0.3 ns per call is about one cycle at 3 GHz: suspect deleted work.

definition: A clock that never goes backwards, unaffected by system time adjustments, suitable for measuring intervals. Python's time.perf_counter() is one.
Python's high-resolution monotonic timer for measuring short intervals.
Python's standard module for timing small snippets by running them many times; it disables garbage collection by default.
A benchmark that times one small piece of code in isolation. Easy to get wrong because of warm-up, dead-code elimination and frequency changes.
An instruction the core has finished and committed, as opposed to work done speculatively and discarded. IPC counts retired instructions.
A CPython 3.12+ option on supported Linux builds that lets perf show Python function names in its profiles.
Hardware entries that track outstanding cache misses, limiting how many memory requests one core can have in flight at once.
The x86 instruction that adds packed single-precision floats lane by lane: four with 128-bit SSE (addps), eight with 256-bit AVX ymm registers, sixteen with AVX-512.
example: vaddps ymm0, ymm1, ymm2 adds eight float pairs.

definition: A group of separate computers connected by a network and used together as one parallel machine; a classic MIMD system.
Compiler output saying which loops were vectorised and why others were not, e.g. GCC -fopt-info-vec-missed or Clang -Rpass-missed=loop-vectorize.
A database that stores each column's values together rather than each row's, a structure-of-arrays layout that suits scans and SIMD.
The fixed time to start a GPU kernel, often microseconds, which can dominate tiny kernels.
Running a vector or warp instruction with some lanes switched off by a mask so they keep their old values. Used for loop tails and for branches that lanes disagree on.
The SM hardware that picks, each cycle, a ready warp and issues its next instruction.
The network of wires and configurable switches in an FPGA that connects logic blocks as the bitstream specifies.
10^-12 joules, a unit used for the energy of single arithmetic operations and memory accesses.
The SI unit of energy; one watt for one second. Accelerator efficiency is often operations per joule.
Deferring loading of code or data until first use, which makes the first run slower.
Short for floating point, as in FP32 or FP reduction semantics.
A cache that keeps serving other requests while one or more misses are outstanding, letting later loads complete before earlier ones.
The company that designs NVIDIA GPUs and the CUDA platform discussed in this module.
Terabytes per second: 10^12 bytes per second, 1,000 GB/s. Modern GPU memory bandwidth is quoted in it.

A processor, such as an ordinary CPU core, built to run any program by fetching and executing instructions one after another, rather than being specialised for one kind of work. Its flexibility costs energy in instruction control and data movement.

A chain of hardware stages separated by registers, each doing part of a computation, so a new input can enter before earlier ones have finished. On an FPGA or ASIC it is built directly from logic, with no instructions to fetch; its throughput is set by the initiation interval and clock, its latency by the number of stages.
example: A 300 MHz pipeline that accepts one packet per cycle handles 300 million packets a second, however many stages deep it is.

definition: A build of a program compiled for debugging, usually with optimisation turned off (for example GCC's -O0 -g) and sometimes extra checks enabled. It can run several times slower than a release build, so timing it says little about production performance.
